newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST-U.S. trade gap seen narrowing in August.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-U.S. trade gap seen narrowing in August.

text.p: The U.S. international trade position should have improved in August, but if the trade deficit resembles July's chasm it could foreshadow a major contraction in third-quarter economic growth, economists said.

The trade data for good and services, due to be released at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT on Friday, October 18, is expected to shrink to $8.5 billion from an eight-and-a-half year high of $11.68 billion in July, according to a Reuters poll of economists.

"Anything close to the July level would lead to a significant downgrade of gross domestic product (GDP) forecasts for Q3," said David Resler, chief economist at Nomura Securities International Inc. "We don't expect that to happen."
Economists said they were puzzled by the wide July deficit and some said there may be a systematic weakness in the seasonal adjustment of July export figures.
The 3.6 percent drop in exports in July should be offset by a 3.7 percent jump in August exports, said Resler.
Exports of civilian aircraft are expected to show strength, recovering somewhat from a 44 percent drop in July.
On the other side of the ledger, the low level of customs duties implies that imports may have come off in August.
"Also, oil imports have not increased and prices have actually dropped slightly from July to August," said Sung Won Sohn, chief economist at Norwest Corp.
Weak domestic demand may play a role in reversing July's 1.2 percent import increase, said forecasters.
Some economists expect the US economy to come off the boil, after growing at a 4.7 percent clip in the second quarter, regardless of what the August trade gap reflects on net-exports.
"Growth wasn't that strong in the third quarter but still the economy was expanding," said James Glassman, senior economist at Chase Securities Inc.
But he added "if we're importing that much stuff and exports are weak, the U.S. economy ought to be even weaker than it seems."

Experts forecast the bilateral trade gap with China continued to rise in August but were divided over whether the deficit with Japan stablized or widened again, after jumping almost 33 percent in July.
They said a stronger Mexican economy should have drawn more exports from the U.S. in August.
The overall U.S. service sector surplus is expected to have widened slightly again, after growing 5.8 percent previously.

Experts said the bond markets could respond vigorously to a worse-than-expected trade deficit, especially if it is in the double digits again. A deficit of around $10 billion would probably lead to about a 0.5 percent decrease in everybody's GDP forecast, Resler said.
